title: In CT-based models of adult heads, eyelid light probes did not see more orbitofrontal grey matter than forehead probes overall, and ultrasound through the orbital roof was close to 3T fMRI
abstract: Light probes on the closed eyelid were not shown to see more of the orbitofrontal cortex than probes on the forehead, and ultrasound sent through the eye socket imaged it only about as well as 3T functional MRI. This matters because the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is important for reward and psychiatric research but is hard to measure: functional MRI loses signal there, and the eye socket looks like a natural opening to it. We built tissue models of the eye sockets from public head CT scans (CQ500) and calculated near-infrared light transport (Monte Carlo, 830 nm) and ultrasound transmission (an elastic-plate model of the bony roof of the eye socket with a Doppler noise model, within FDA eye-exposure limits). Here OFC means grey matter within 10 mm of that roof, and 'share' means the fraction of the detected light path that lies in OFC. In 18 heads, the pre-specified eyelid-to-forehead light channel had 0.35 times (95% CI 0.23-0.54) the OFC share of a forehead channel just above the brow. Over all pairs 30-40 mm apart, the eyelid/forehead ratio was 0.97 (0.85-1.32). Eyelid pairs possibly reached the middle OFC slightly better (about 1.2 times; 95% CI 0.94-1.47), no pair reached its posterior third, and pairs with both optodes on the eyelid saw almost no OFC. The light comparison depends on how sinus air cells are modelled (with absorbing air cells the pre-specified ratio rose to 1.2 in 3 heads; with reflecting walls it was 0.72 in 2 heads). Per watt, eyelid light sources put 0.18 times as much light into OFC as forehead sources, but more selectively. For ultrasound in 75 orbits, the roof was 1.0 mm of compact-bone equivalent and the sound met it at about 50 degrees. The smallest voxel that detected a 10% blood-volume change in 60 s was 3.1 mm (10-90% over orbits 2.2-4.3), against 2.9 mm for 3T and 1.5 mm for 7T functional MRI with OFC signal loss. Ultrasound was better than 3T in 39% of the OFC of a typical orbit (21-44% over assumed 3T signal losses) and better than 7T in 5%. An independent review found an error in the roof thickness and a missing focusing limit; both are corrected. Main limitation: these are model results; the in vivo attenuation of the thin roof, eye movement and the geometric OFC definition are untested.
